analysis.one_liner: Replaces the 1872 free-mining system with leases, royalties up to 12.5%, and mine cleanup guarantees.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote, expiring when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Under an 1872 law, anyone can stake a mining claim on federal land, take the gold, copper, or silver, pay no royalty to the government, and in some cases buy the land outright. This bill would close that system: federal land would be leased, not claimed for free, with royalties of up to 12.5 percent of production value, permits with reclamation plans, cleanup bonds paid up front, bans on mining in parks and protected areas, and a fund to clean up tens of thousands of abandoned mines that pollute western water.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently receive nothing when companies extract billions in gold, copper, and other metals from public land; western communities and tribes whose water and sacred sites are threatened by mining and abandoned mine pollution; and states, which would get 25 percent of the new royalty revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Closes all federal land to new free mining claims; hardrock mining would proceed only through prospecting licenses and leases issued by the Interior Department.

Imposes a royalty of at least 12.5 percent of gross production value on new mining leases and at least 8 percent on existing operations, with 25 percent of revenue going to the states and the rest to a new Hardrock Mining Reclamation Fund.

Requires operators to post financial assurance covering the full cost of reclamation, including long-term water treatment, before any mining begins, and bars permits to companies with unresolved environmental violations.

Bans new mining in wilderness study areas, areas of critical environmental concern, National Conservation System units, and inventoried roadless areas, and prohibits permits that would impair national parks or monuments.
Creates a Hardrock Mining Reclamation Fund, financed by royalties, fees, and penalties, to clean up abandoned hardrock mines.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies, which would pay royalties on production for the first time, annual per-claim fees, application and rental charges, and the full up-front cost of cleanup bonds; existing mines are grandfathered at a lower 8 percent royalty and can finish under approved plans.

drawbacks.text: The royalty and permitting requirements would raise the cost of producing gold, copper, and other metals on federal land, which critics argue could push some production and jobs overseas or raise prices for domestically supplied minerals.

Existing mines are grandfathered: they pay only an 8 percent royalty and can complete operations under previously approved plans, so the bill would not change the economics of mines already operating when it passed.

The bill exempts small miners with under $50,000 in annual mineral income from royalties and fees entirely, an exemption based on self-certification that could be gamed by structuring related-party holdings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is large and direct: royalties on minerals extracted from land the public owns, cleanup money for abandoned mine sites that now leak acid and metals into western rivers, and real cleanup bonds instead of leaving reclamation costs to taxpayers. The costs fall almost entirely on mining companies, whose current arrangement is a leftover of an 1872 statute written before modern mining and modern environmental law. The main honest criticism is the grandfathering, which leaves existing mines largely on their old terms, and the risk that higher costs shift some production abroad; those are real but do not come close to offsetting the gains, since the minerals belong to the public either way.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on May 10, 2018, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
On May 30, 2018, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it stayed.
The bill had 21 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors.
No further action was recorded, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies are better off because the bill died: they continue to extract gold, copper, and other metals from federal land without paying royalties, under cleanup and bonding rules far weaker than the bill would have imposed.

for.name: Raúl Grijalva
for.role: U.S. Representative (AZ-3), sponsor and ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and recruited 15 original House cosponsors for it.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee majority
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.role: Gold, copper, and other hardrock producers operating under the 1872 Mining Law
against.what_they_did: Opposed hardrock mining reform, including royalty proposals of this kind, throughout the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 21 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican committee majority took no action on it.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, copper, silver, and other locatable minerals)
industries.note: The bill would end their free access to federal minerals under the 1872 Mining Law, charge royalties of 8 to 12.5 percent for the first time, and require them to post the full cost of cleanup before mining. Today the public gets no royalty on these minerals and often inherits the cleanup bill when mines are abandoned.
The bill carves out small miners with under $50,000 in annual mineral income, who could convert claims to leases with low rentals, no royalties, and no claim maintenance fees.

industries.industry: Mine reclamation and environmental remediation contractors
industries.note: The new reclamation fund would finance cleanup of abandoned hardrock mines, creating paid remediation work in western states.
